source.title: Red, Amber, or Green? Athlete Monitoring in Team Sport: The Need for Decision-Support Systems

paper.citation: Robertson, S., Bartlett, J. D., & Gastin, P. B. (2017). Red, amber, or green? Athlete monitoring in team sport: The need for decision-support systems. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 12(Suppl 2), S2-73–S2-79. https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2016-0541
paper.abstract: What data, analysis, threshold, visualization, and implementation choices should practitioners consider when using traffic-light athlete-monitoring systems in team sport? This is a narrative brief review and practitioner framework, not an empirical evaluation with a defined athlete sample. Examples draw primarily from team-sport monitoring, including Australian football and other elite environments. The authors synthesize decision-support concepts, measurement literature, applied examples, and illustrative training-load data. No systematic search, risk-of-bias assessment, prospective validation, or comparison of traffic-light systems is reported.
paper.tldr: This brief review explains why red–amber–green dashboards are not self-validating and offers a framework for selecting data, setting individualized thresholds, representing uncertainty, and communicating flags as decision support. Framework proposition, not an empirical finding: traffic-light systems provide rapid visual summaries, but evidence for their objective decision-support value is scarce and operationalization lacks standardization. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: The authors synthesize decision-support concepts, measurement literature, applied examples, and illustrative training-load data. No systematic search, risk-of-bias assessment, prospective validation, or comparison of traffic-light systems is reported.
paper.findings: Framework proposition, not an empirical finding: traffic-light systems provide rapid visual summaries, but evidence for their objective decision-support value is scarce and operationalization lacks standardization. Traffic-light outputs are limited as predictive tools because injury and performance outcomes occur after the decision, events are sparse or variable, and large historical datasets are required. Data inclusion should be driven by validity, reliability, nonredundancy, decision relevance, and collection burden rather than availability alone. Individual and group normalization, raw values, z-scores, and percentage change can support different inferences; conversion may improve comparison while reducing interpretability or creating unstable values near zero. Different definitions of meaningful change, including SD, coefficient of variation, smallest worthwhile change, and effect-size approaches, produce different flags and potential actions for the same data. The paper’s CV-based green/amber/red thresholds are explicitly an illustration, not validated universal cut points. Effective displays should show individual and group patterns and make outliers, anomalies, and trends interpretable to intended users.
paper.limitations: The review does not demonstrate that traffic lights improve training decisions, athlete availability, performance, or injury outcomes. Color categories compress continuous, uncertain information and can imply categorical certainty, causality, or urgency that the underlying evidence does not support. Thresholds derived from short baselines can be unstable and may combine measurement error, biological variation, adaptation, and context. Red–amber–green alone is not accessible for all users with color-vision deficiency and should be paired with text, symbols, values, and uncertainty. Injury incidence is an unsuitable sole validator for routine flags, and restrictive systems may unnecessarily remove training exposure. Collegiate American-football implementation requires position-, phase-, drill-, and role-specific validation plus explicit accountability for any action.
paper.practicalImplications: Use traffic-light status as a prompt for structured review, not an automatic prescription. Display the observed value, athlete-specific reference, uncertainty, direction and size of change, missing-data status, and relevant context beside any color. Predefine who reviews a flag, what follow-up information is required, and which actions are reversible. Audit false alarms, missed concerns, overrides, and downstream decisions so the system can be recalibrated.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use traffic-light status as a prompt for structured review, not an automatic prescription. Display the observed value, athlete-specific reference, uncertainty, direction and size of change, missing-data status, and relevant context beside any color. Predefine who reviews a flag, what follow-up information is required, and which actions are reversible. Audit false alarms, missed concerns, overrides, and downstream decisions so the system can be recalibrated. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
